sentences: Burned once by a forged provenance, the museum was chary of private sellers.
He was chary with praise and generous with everything else.
The coach chastised the squad for a lapse that lasted four seconds and cost the season.
She chastised herself for the error long after everyone else had forgotten it.

chauvinism.definition: excessive loyalty to one's own group
sentences: Nicolas Chauvin's fanatical devotion to Napoleon gave the world a word for it.
Culinary chauvinism insists no country abroad has ever seasoned anything correctly.

chauvinist.definition: one who believes their group is superior
sentences: The chauvinist praised local engineering while driving an imported car.
Every chauvinist believes the accident of his birthplace was a verdict.

chauvinistic.definition: aggressively convinced of one's group's superiority
sentences: The chauvinistic editorial insulted three neighboring countries in a single paragraph.
Chauvinistic pride survives entirely on not looking anywhere else.

check.definition: to restrain or halt the progress of
sentences: Only a cold spring checked an insect population that had doubled every year.
Checks and balances exist because power, left alone, does not check itself.

checkered.definition: marked by both successes and failures
sentences: He arrived with a checkered past and a genuinely impressive set of references.
The firm's checkered history included two bankruptcies and one Nobel laureate.
She cherished the battered dictionary more than the prizes on the shelf above it.
We cherish what we might lose; nobody cherishes tap water.
Legal chicanery delayed the trial until the key witness had moved abroad.
The contract's chicanery lived entirely in a footnote about renewal.
She chided him for skipping breakfast, then handed him half of hers.
Chiding is scolding with the affection still switched on.
Cheap fusion power remained a chimera through four decades of confident forecasts.
The original chimera had a lion's head, a goat's body, and no chance of existing.

chivalrous.definition: courteous and honorable, especially toward others
sentences: His chivalrous gesture at the door lost some charm when he let it swing back.
Chivalrous conduct was invented by knights who mostly did the opposite.
The choleric conductor snapped his baton twice in one rehearsal.
Medieval medicine blamed choleric tempers on yellow bile; modern offices blame email.

chortle.definition: to laugh in a gleeful, snorting way
sentences: He chortled at his own joke before the punch line, which spoiled it entirely.
Lewis Carroll invented chortle by welding chuckle to snort.
The exhibit's chronological order made a two-century argument in a single corridor.
His account was chronological, thorough, and missing the only afternoon that mattered.
It would be churlish to complain about a free upgrade, so he complained quietly.
A churlish reply to a kind letter says everything about the writer.
After ten minutes of circumlocution he admitted the money was gone.
Circumlocution means talking around; the word itself takes six syllables to say so.
The new rules circumscribed the agency's power without reducing its budget.
Her role was carefully circumscribed and gradually, quietly, ignored.
Within his circumscribed authority he did remarkable things; beyond it, nothing.
A circumscribed study of one village produced the decade's broadest conclusion.
Circumspect in public and blunt in private, she survived four administrations.
The word means looking around, which is what caution physically resembles.
Under different circumstances the same decision would have been called courageous.
He explained the circumstances at length and never once mentioned his own part in them.

circumvent.definition: to get around a rule or obstacle cleverly
sentences: The shell company existed solely to circumvent a law written the previous spring.
Every new rule creates a small industry devoted to circumventing it.

cite.definition: to quote or refer to as evidence
sentences: He cited four studies, none of which said what he claimed they said.
Cite your sources, or someone eventually will cite them against you.
The tower is clad in copper that has spent a century turning green.
Clad only in a raincoat and confidence, he addressed the press.

clamber.definition: to climb awkwardly using hands and feet
sentences: They clambered over the rocks with all the grace of falling furniture.
He clambered up the ranks by routes nobody else considered dignified.

clamor.definition: loud noise or vehement public demand
sentences: The clamor for an inquiry grew louder than the scandal that had started it.
A clamor outside the chamber ended a debate no argument could.
Clamorous gulls made the harbor unusable for anyone hoping to think.
The clamorous minority got the interview; the silent majority got the bill.

clandestine.definition: kept secret, especially for illicit reasons
sentences: Their clandestine meetings were held in a café directly opposite the ministry.
Clandestine funding built the road; nobody would say which country's.
The clangor of the foundry set the whole street's windows vibrating.
Church bells produce clangor; alarm clocks produce something less forgivable.
The report was a clarion call that four committees agreed to study further.
Her clarion voice carried to the back of a hall built before microphones.

cleave.definition: to split apart, or to cling to
sentences: Cleave is its own opposite: an axe cleaves wood, and a vine cleaves to the wall.
The party cleaved into two factions that cleaved stubbornly to the same name.
The governor granted clemency an hour before the sentence was to be carried out.
Clemency also describes mild weather, since both spare you what was coming.
One phone call clinched a deal that eighteen months of dinners had not.
The final witness clinched the case in eleven minutes of testimony.
The policy cloaked a cut in the language of reform.
Fog cloaked the harbor so completely that the ferry docked by memory.
The film's cloying score told the audience how to feel every eleven seconds.
One spoonful is delightful; the whole jar is cloying.

coagulate.definition: to thicken into a semisolid mass
sentences: Blood coagulates in seconds, which is the only reason paper cuts are survivable.
The group's vague complaints slowly coagulated into a formal petition.

coalesce.definition: to come together to form a whole
sentences: Scattered protests coalesced into a movement with a name and a bank account.
The notes coalesced into an argument only after the third rewrite.
He coasted through the first year and met the second one at full speed.
The company coasted on one invention for eleven years.
She coaxed the engine into starting with a technique the manual did not describe.
You cannot coax a deadline, though everyone tries.

coda.definition: a concluding section or final addition
sentences: The last chapter is a coda: nothing happens, and everything is finally explained.
His retirement speech was a coda to a career that had ended, quietly, years earlier.
The startup was coddled by investors until its first honest quarter.
Coddle an egg gently in water; coddle a person and you get something less useful.

codicil.definition: an addition or supplement to a will
sentences: A codicil written three days before his death redirected the entire estate.
The codicil was valid, witnessed, and written in crayon, which delighted the lawyers.

coercion.definition: the use of force or threats to compel
sentences: A confession obtained by coercion is worthless in court and in life.
Coercion gets you compliance today and sabotage every day after.

coercive.definition: using force or threats to compel
sentences: The contract's coercive clause was struck out by a judge who called it "remarkable."
Coercive measures work quickly and expire the moment attention wanders.

coffer.definition: a chest for valuables; financial reserves
sentences: The city's coffers were empty, and the fountain still needed repairing.
Three centuries of donations filled the coffers of a chapel that seats forty.
Her cogent two-page rebuttal ended a debate that had run for two years.
Cogent arguments change votes; loud ones only change the volume.
He cogitated over the problem for a week and solved it on a bus.
To cogitate is to think slowly enough that people notice you doing it.
English "father" and Latin "pater" are cognate, which is why the pattern repeats everywhere.
The two disciplines are cognate and have not spoken since 1974.
Fully cognizant of the risk, she signed anyway and said so in writing.
The board was cognizant of the deficit and unwilling to name it.

cohere.definition: to hold together logically or physically
sentences: The essay's parts never quite cohere, though each is fine alone.
Wet sand coheres; dry sand has opinions of its own.
A cohesive team of average players beat a fractured team of stars.
The chapter is cohesive; the book around it is a filing cabinet.

cohort.definition: a group sharing a characteristic or time
sentences: The 1994 cohort produced three ministers and one very famous defendant.
A Roman cohort was six hundred soldiers; a research cohort is six hundred spreadsheets.
Her coiffure survived the storm better than the umbrella did.
The portrait was commissioned mainly to document the coiffure.

coin.definition: to invent a new word or phrase
sentences: Shakespeare coined "assassination," which is a striking gift to leave a language.
The phrase was coined in a memo and lived to embarrass three generations.

collaborate.definition: to work jointly; to cooperate with an enemy
sentences: They collaborated for a decade and never once agreed on the first paragraph.
The word carries a shadow: in wartime, to collaborate meant something unforgivable.

collation.definition: the act of collecting and comparing texts
sentences: Collation of the manuscripts revealed a missing line in every printed edition.
The collation took four months and changed one word.

collude.definition: to cooperate secretly for a wrongful purpose
sentences: The three suppliers colluded to fix a price nobody could afford to refuse.
To collude is to cooperate with the lights off.

collusion.definition: secret cooperation for a dishonest purpose
sentences: The identical bids, down to a typo, suggested collusion rather than coincidence.
Collusion is the crime that requires two people to keep one secret.
One bad experience colored her view of the entire profession.
The witness's memory was colored by six months of newspaper coverage.
The Colossus of Rhodes gave us the adjective and then fell over in an earthquake.
It was a colossal error, executed with impressive attention to detail.
The chamber's comity survived until the cameras were installed.
Comity between nations means recognizing each other's courts without being forced to.
Proceedings commenced at nine and adjourned, unresolved, at nine forty.
Graduation is called commencement because it names the beginning, not the ending.
Her commendable honesty about the failure was the reason she kept the job.
"Commendable effort" on a report is praise with a small knife in it.
The punishment was not commensurate with an offense involving one traffic cone.
Salary commensurate with experience is a phrase that means bring your own leverage.

commiserate.definition: to express sympathy for another's misfortune
sentences: They commiserated over identical rejection letters and split a very large dessert.
Commiserating is grief shared until it becomes portable.

commission.definition: to formally order or authorize work
sentences: The city commissioned a study, received it, and commissioned a second one.
She was commissioned to paint the hall and given nine days.

commit.definition: to pledge oneself; to carry out an act
sentences: He committed to the plan in public and hedged it in every email afterward.
One word covers marrying, memorizing, and murdering, which is English at its strangest.

compel.definition: to force or drive to do something
sentences: The court compelled disclosure of documents the firm had described as nonexistent.
Curiosity compelled her to open the box the label warned against.
The evidence was compelling enough that even the defense stopped objecting.
A compelling first chapter forgives a great deal of what follows.
The compendium fit two centuries of case law into four hundred pages.
His notebook was a compendium of other people's best ideas, carefully attributed.
Competent is the highest compliment some professions ever need.
A competent surgeon beats a brilliant one with a bad night's sleep.

complacent.definition: smugly satisfied and unaware of danger
sentences: Three good years made the company complacent and the fourth one instructive.
Complacent is not the same as content: one has stopped looking, the other has stopped wanting.
Her complaisance was mistaken for weakness by everyone who later worked for her.
Complaisance pleases; complacence sleeps. One letter, two very different failings.
A complaisant assistant said yes to four impossible deadlines in one morning.
He was complaisant with superiors and remarkably firm with everyone else.

complement.definition: to complete or enhance by adding
sentences: The wine complemented the fish, which is the only sentence sommeliers actually need.
Her caution complemented his recklessness for exactly one profitable year.

complementary.definition: combining well to form a whole
sentences: Their complementary skills covered everything except deciding who was in charge.
Complementary completes; complimentary flatters — and only one is free.
A compliant workforce is easy to manage and impossible to learn anything from.
The building was fully compliant with a code written before elevators.
Silence in that room was not neutral; it was complicit.
He was complicit by signature, which the court found sufficient.

comply.definition: to act in accordance with a rule or request
sentences: They complied with the letter of the order and buried its purpose entirely.
Comply first, complain in writing afterward: the bureaucrat's survival rule.

comport.definition: to behave in a specified way; to agree with
sentences: He comported himself with dignity through a hearing designed to remove it.
The testimony did not comport with the timeline the phone records established.

compound.definition: to make worse by adding to
sentences: He compounded the error by explaining it at length on television.
Interest compounds, and so does neglect.
The comprehensive review took two years and confirmed what the interns said in week one.
Comprehensive insurance covers everything except what happened to you.

compromise.definition: to settle by concession; to endanger
sentences: They compromised on everything except the one clause that mattered.
A single reused password compromised the entire system.
She conceded the point graciously and won the argument twenty minutes later.
He conceded the election before the last district had finished counting.

conceit.definition: excessive pride; a fanciful literary device
sentences: His conceit was so complete that criticism registered as jealousy.
The novel's central conceit is that the house remembers everyone who lived there.

concept.definition: an abstract idea or general notion
sentences: The concept survived four redesigns and one complete change of purpose.
"Fairness" is a concept everyone endorses and nobody defines the same way.

concern.definition: worry, or a matter of interest
sentences: Her only concern was whether anyone would read past the summary.
The auditors expressed concern, which in their language is a scream.
He tried to conciliate both factions and was distrusted by each for it.
A small apology conciliated a neighbor who had been silently furious for years.
His conciliatory tone surprised a room that had prepared for a fight.
A conciliatory gesture costs little and is remembered for years.
The DNA result was conclusive, which the four eyewitnesses had never been.
Nothing in that field is conclusive; it merely becomes expensive to disagree.
Growth came with the concomitant traffic that nobody had budgeted for.
Fame and its concomitant loss of privacy arrive as a package deal.
Three judges concurred with the outcome and disagreed about every reason for it.
The experts concur, which historically means check again in ten years.

condemn.definition: to express strong disapproval; to sentence
sentences: The building was condemned, which was the first official acknowledgment of the smell.
He condemned the practice in public and continued it in the accounts.

condolence.definition: an expression of sympathy for grief
sentences: The letter of condolence arrived a month late and was worth the wait.
Condolences are easiest to give and hardest to phrase.

condone.definition: to overlook or tacitly accept wrongdoing
sentences: The board did not condone the conduct; it merely declined to notice it twice.
To explain is not to condone, though the distinction rarely survives a headline.

conducive.definition: tending to promote or help bring about
sentences: An open-plan office is conducive to conversation and hostile to concentration.
Nothing about the schedule was conducive to actually finishing anything.
His conduct at the hearing was faultless, which made the evidence worse.
The code of conduct ran forty pages and omitted the situation that arose.

confer.definition: to grant, or to consult together
sentences: The degree confers a title and no useful powers whatsoever.
They conferred in the corridor for ninety seconds and reversed a year of policy.
A dropped lamp became a conflagration that redrew the city's map.
The dispute grew from a memo into a conflagration involving four departments.

conflate.definition: to merge two distinct things confusingly
sentences: The article conflates correlation and cause, then builds a policy on top.
Do not conflate being busy with being useful; the calendar cannot tell the difference.
The city grew at the confluence of two rivers and one very old road.
A confluence of cheap credit and bad memory produced the bubble.
The result confounded a theory that three textbooks had already printed.
Weather confounded the forecast, the schedule, and the caterers.
The gravy congealed while the argument about politics reached its second hour.
Vague resentment congealed into a formal complaint sometime that winter.

congenial.definition: pleasant and agreeable in company or nature
sentences: The library was congenial to thought and hostile to conversation, which suited him.
They made congenial neighbors for nine years and never once entered each other's houses.

conjectural.definition: based on guesswork rather than evidence
sentences: The reconstruction is conjectural: two walls survive, and the rest is confident drawing.
His dating of the manuscript remains conjectural and is quoted as fact.
Conjugal duties in the old law codes were listed alongside property and cattle.
Their conjugal arrangement involved two cities and one very reliable train.

conjure.definition: to summon or produce as if by magic
sentences: He conjured a budget out of nothing and a resignation out of the treasurer.
The smell of pine conjures a specific December he has never described to anyone.
The conniving deputy leaked one paragraph and toppled a minister.
Conniving requires patience, which is why it so rarely fails.

connoisseur.definition: an expert judge in matters of taste
sentences: A connoisseur can name the vineyard; the rest of us can name the color.
He was a connoisseur of bureaucratic excuses and had a favorite.

connotation.definition: an implied meaning beyond the literal
sentences: "Thrifty" and "stingy" denote the same behavior with opposite connotations.
The word's connotation had drifted so far that the dictionary gave up.

connote.definition: to imply in addition to the literal meaning
sentences: "Home" denotes a residence and connotes everything the residence is not.
The uniform connotes authority even when its wearer is nineteen and lost.

conscientious.definition: careful, thorough, and guided by principle
sentences: A conscientious editor caught the error on page four hundred and eleven.
Conscientious objectors accepted prison rather than a rifle, which required its own courage.

consecrate.definition: to declare sacred; to dedicate solemnly
sentences: The ground was consecrated in 1103 and paved over in 1974.
He consecrated thirty years to a dictionary that reached the letter G.
The consensus formed in the corridor and was ratified, ceremonially, in the room.
Scientific consensus is not a vote; it is what survives repeated attempts to break it.
The most consequential decision of the decade was made by four people on a Friday.
Small consequential changes beat large ceremonial ones every time.

conservatory.definition: a music school, or a glass-walled room for plants
sentences: She trained at a conservatory where practicing after midnight was a tradition, not a rule.
The conservatory held four hundred plants and one very confused cat.

consider.definition: to think about carefully; to regard as
sentences: Consider the alternatives before announcing that there are none.
He considered himself misunderstood; his colleagues considered him understood perfectly.
Nothing consoled her until a colleague admitted making the same mistake in 1998.
He consoled the team by pointing out how much worse it could have been, which did not help.
They consolidated six databases into one and lost only two years of records.
He spent the first term consolidating power and the second wondering what for.
He was conspicuous by his absence, which is the loudest way to attend.
Conspicuous consumption is spending designed to be seen, not enjoyed.

conspire.definition: to plot secretly; to combine toward an effect
sentences: Rain, roadworks, and a lost key conspired to make him forty minutes late.
They conspired for months and were undone by one enthusiastic group email.
A constant friend and an inconstant correspondent, he wrote twice a decade.
The only constant in the department was the coffee machine's failure.
To the consternation of the organizers, the guest of honor brought a rival.
The announcement produced consternation in the office and celebration in the pub.

constituency.definition: a body of supporters or voters
sentences: The policy had no constituency except the person who wrote it.
Her constituency was small, loyal, and impossible to poll accurately.
Break the compound into its constituents and the mystery becomes chemistry.
He answered every constituent letter personally, which is why he had no evenings.
Three missed payments constitute default, whatever the customer intended.
Women constituted a majority of the workforce and a fifth of its management.
Constrained by budget and pride, they rebuilt the roof themselves, badly.
His constrained smile in the photograph tells the story the caption omits.
The only real constraint was time, which is the only one that cannot be negotiated.
Poets choose constraints deliberately, which is either discipline or masochism.
Cold constricts the blood vessels, which is why fingers go white before they hurt.
New rules constricted lending until the smallest firms stopped applying.

construe.definition: to interpret in a particular way
sentences: Silence was construed as consent by everyone who benefited from that reading.
The clause can be construed two ways, and both parties chose the profitable one.
A consummate professional, she rewrote the speech in the car and delivered it flawlessly.
He is a consummate bore, which requires as much dedication as any other mastery.

consumption.definition: the using up of resources; an old term for tuberculosis
sentences: Water consumption fell eight percent when the meters became visible in the kitchen.
Nineteenth-century novels killed off half their heroines with consumption.
Familiarity breeds contempt, and so does reading the minutes of any committee.
He was held in contempt of court for laughing, which was accurate and unwise.
A contemptuous glance at the proposal was the only feedback ever received.
Contemptible earns the scorn; contemptuous delivers it.

contend.definition: to assert; to compete or struggle
sentences: She contends that the data were misread, and three replications now agree.
Four teams contended for a title that was decided by weather.

contention.definition: an assertion in an argument; dispute
sentences: His central contention survived the review; his evidence did not.
The border remained a point of contention for two centuries and one afternoon of talks.

contentious.definition: causing or likely to cause argument
sentences: The most contentious clause was three words long.
A contentious colleague can make even the coffee order a constitutional matter.
The forty-eight contiguous states leave Alaska and Hawaii permanently in the footnote.
Their offices were contiguous, and they communicated exclusively by email.
Funding was contingent on results that required the funding to produce.
Every plan was contingent on a ferry that ran when it felt like it.

contract.definition: to shrink; to acquire an illness
sentences: Metal contracts in the cold, which is why the bridge sings in January.
He contracted a fever abroad and a lifelong distrust of buffet tables.
Blake believed contraries were necessary: without opposition there is no progression.
The two policies were contraries dressed in the same vocabulary.

contravene.definition: to violate a law or rule
sentences: The sale contravened a statute that everyone had assumed was repealed.
To contravene is to go against, in the literal Latin sense of walking the other way.
A small contretemps over seating consumed the first hour of the summit.
The contretemps at the buffet was later described in three memoirs, differently.
He looked contrite until the cameras left the room.
A contrite apology names the harm; the other kind names the misunderstanding.
The statement offered explanations where contrition was expected.
Contrition is measured in changed behavior, never in adjectives.
She contrived to be seated next to the one person who could sign the check.
He contrived a solution from two paperclips and a genuinely dangerous amount of confidence.
The ending was contrived: three coincidences arriving in a single afternoon.
His contrived spontaneity took two assistants and a schedule.
The contumacious witness was fined daily and enjoyed every minute of it.
Contumacious silence in court is expensive and, occasionally, principled.
The report listed contusions, a sprain, and a strong opinion about the referee.
Contusion is what medicine calls a bruise when it wants to be paid more.
The conundrum was scheduling: everyone was free at exactly no common hour.
A riddle has an answer; a conundrum has a committee.
He convalesced for six weeks and wrote the best chapter of his career.
The company convalesced slowly, one quiet quarter at a time.
The convalescent patient was ordered to rest and immediately reorganized the ward's library.
A convalescent economy still walks with a stick.

convention.definition: an accepted custom, or a large assembly
sentences: Convention required a black tie; the invitation required nothing of the sort.
The convention filled four hotels and produced one memorable sentence.
The conventional wisdom was wrong for six years and then, briefly, right.
A conventional solution nobody argues with beats a brilliant one nobody adopts.

converge.definition: to come together from different directions
sentences: Three independent methods converged on the same number, which is how facts get made.
The roads converge at a roundabout that has defeated two generations of drivers.
Conversant in four languages and fluent in none, he traveled cheerfully anyway.
She was conversant with the regulations and openly contemptuous of them.
Cheap credit fuels growth; conversely, its withdrawal ends the party abruptly.
He hated crowds and, conversely, could not bear an empty house.

conversion.definition: a change from one form or belief to another
sentences: The conversion of the mill into flats took three years and one heroic architect.
His conversion to caution came directly after a very expensive lesson.

conviction.definition: a firm belief; a formal guilty verdict
sentences: He argued with the conviction of a man who had not checked.
The conviction was overturned after eleven years and one persistent journalist.

convince.definition: to cause someone to believe something
sentences: Data convinced nobody; one anecdote convinced everyone.
He convinced himself first, which is always the hardest audience to leave.
The convivial dinner ran four hours and settled nothing on the agenda.
Convivial comes from living together — the word was always about the table.

convoke.definition: to call together for a meeting
sentences: The dean convoked the faculty at short notice, which itself announced bad news.
Parliaments are convoked, and occasionally regret answering.

convoluted.definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
sentences: The plot was so convoluted that the actors kept a chart backstage.
Convoluted rules protect whoever wrote them.
She took copious notes and could never find the one line she needed.
Copious evidence, poorly organized, loses to one clear page.
Relations stayed cordial, which is diplomatic for nobody has shouted yet.
A cordial greeting from someone who has just read your review is a small miracle.
The archive was a cornucopia of misfiled letters and one forgotten treaty.
The horn of plenty came from a goat that fed the infant Zeus, which seems a raw deal.
A corollary of open data is that mistakes become public property.
Fame's corollary is a mailbox nobody can answer.
The ghost story works because the footprints are stubbornly corporeal.
His corporeal needs were three coffees and a chair by the window.
The corpulent cat refused every diet and outlived two veterinarians.
Corpulent is the polite word, which is why it appears in wills and portraits.
Ice cream sales correlate with drownings, and neither causes the other.
The two datasets correlate beautifully and explain nothing.
A parking ticket corroborated an alibi that nobody had believed.
One witness asserts; two corroborate; three usually contradict each other.

corrosion.definition: gradual destruction, especially by chemical action
sentences: Corrosion had eaten the bolts, and the inspection had been scheduled for next spring.
The slow corrosion of trust rarely announces itself until something falls.

cosmopolitan.definition: worldly; at home in many cultures
sentences: The port was cosmopolitan a century before the capital learned the word.
Cosmopolitan tastes and a provincial budget make for interesting weekends.
The team cosseted its star until he could no longer tolerate ordinary weather.
Cosset originally meant a lamb raised by hand, which explains the tone.
A cosseted childhood left him unprepared for a queue.
The cosseted prototype worked perfectly in a room built for it alone.
A coterie of six decided which poems the century would remember.
Every coterie thinks of itself as a movement.

coterminous.definition: having the same boundaries or duration
sentences: The parish and the county were coterminous until a boundary review invented three exceptions.
His tenure was coterminous with the building's only functional decade.
The board would not countenance a delay, having already announced the date.
As a noun it means the face; as a verb, keeping a straight one while permitting something.

counterintuitive.definition: contrary to what common sense suggests
sentences: The counterintuitive result held up: adding a road made the traffic worse.
Most good advice sounds counterintuitive until you have paid for the alternative.
Headquarters countermanded the order four hours after the trucks had left.
One phone call countermanded a policy three departments had spent a year drafting.

counterpoint.definition: a contrasting element that sets off another
sentences: Her steady prose is the counterpoint to a story that would otherwise be hysterical.
In music, counterpoint is two melodies refusing to yield and somehow agreeing.

counterproductive.definition: having the opposite of the intended effect
sentences: Banning the book was counterproductive: it sold out in a week.
Working eighty hours became counterproductive somewhere around hour fifty.

court.definition: to seek favor or invite something risky
sentences: The airline courted controversy with an advertisement it withdrew in six hours.
He courted investors for a year and disaster in a single afternoon.
The covert operation was described in three memoirs before it was declassified.
Covert hostility in a meeting is far more efficient than the open kind.

covet.definition: to desire something belonging to another
sentences: He coveted the corner office and got it just as the building was sold.
The commandment against coveting is the only one about a feeling.
The crowd was not cowed by the threat and arrived the next day in greater numbers.
He tried to cow the intern, who cited the handbook back at him.
The dog cowered at thunder and hunted wild boar without hesitation.
They cowered behind procedure rather than make a decision.
The company was coy about the launch date and precise about the price.
A coy answer is a refusal wearing a smile.
He cozened the old man out of a farm with a document and a fountain pen.
Cozen is what con artists did before the word "con" existed.

crabbed.definition: irritable; or cramped and hard to read
sentences: His crabbed handwriting hid a generous mind and one very rude marginal note.
A crabbed reply to a friendly email costs more than it saves.
The chair showed craft in every joint and no imagination whatsoever.
Craft cuts both ways: witchcraft and handicraft share the same word.
A crafty amendment buried the exemption in a definition.
The crafty raccoon defeated three locks and one engineer.
The craven retreat was described in the minutes as "a strategic pause."
Craven silence when it mattered is remembered longer than any speech.

credence.definition: belief in or acceptance of something
sentences: The photograph lent credence to a story nobody had believed for thirty years.
Give no credence to a rumor whose source improves with each telling.
Credibility takes a decade to build and one press conference to spend.
The witness lost all credibility over a detail about a bus timetable.
The threat was credible enough to close the airport for four hours.
A credible denial requires details; a guilty one requires adjectives.
A creditable third place, given that half the team had food poisoning.
Creditable means good enough to mention and not good enough to celebrate.

credo.definition: a statement of beliefs or guiding principles
sentences: "Measure twice" was his entire credo, and it built forty houses.
The company credo was printed on mugs and contradicted in every meeting.

credulity.definition: readiness to believe on flimsy evidence
sentences: The scheme relied on credulity and a very convincing letterhead.
The plot twist strains credulity past the point of politeness.
A credulous audience is worth more to a fraud than a rich one.
Credulous means you believe; incredulous means you cannot — one letter, opposite people.

crescendo.definition: a gradual increase toward a peak
sentences: The complaints reached a crescendo the week the elevator finally stopped entirely.
Purists insist a crescendo is the rise, not the peak, and lose that argument daily.
He returned crestfallen from an interview that had gone, he thought, brilliantly.
The image is a bird's crest collapsing — disappointment with feathers.
Ferns grew from a crevice in the wall where nothing should survive.
Every crevice in the argument was probed, and one of them opened.

crew.definition: a group working together, especially on a vessel
sentences: The crew mutinied over food, which is how most mutinies actually start.
A film crew of eighty people waited four hours for one cloud.

crone.definition: a withered old woman, often in folklore
sentences: The fairy tale's crone gives the best advice and is always ignored.
Folklore keeps the crone; history keeps her herbal knowledge under someone else's name.

croon.definition: to sing or speak softly and sentimentally
sentences: He crooned to the engine as though flattery might restart it.
Microphones made crooning possible; before them, singers had to shout.

cryptic.definition: having a hidden or obscure meaning
sentences: The cryptic note said "check the second drawer," and there were nine drawers.
Cryptic crosswords are a national pastime for people who enjoy being insulted by a newspaper.
The plan crystallized on a napkin in a station café at midnight.
Vague unease crystallized into a specific fear when the auditor asked for the second file.

culminate.definition: to reach a climax or final stage
sentences: Twenty years of work culminated in a paper that four people read carefully.
The festival culminates in a bonfire that the fire service watches nervously.
The inquiry established culpability at every level and consequences at none.
Culpability is shared easily and admitted rarely.
The report found the contractor culpable and the supervisor merely unlucky.
Culpable negligence is carelessness the law decided to take personally.
A cultured voice and a savage opinion make a memorable dinner guest.
The cultured pearl is real, grown deliberately — which is also true of most cultured people.
The cumbersome approval process took six weeks to say no.
Early mobile phones were cumbersome enough to double as weapons.
A cunning clause let either party withdraw and only one party knew it.
The cunning fox of fables would, in reality, mostly like to be left alone.
Cupidity, not need, emptied the pension fund.
The word comes from Cupid, whose arrows apparently also hit wallets.
A single tax curbed a habit that four campaigns had failed to touch.
Curb your enthusiasm until the contract is signed.
The office curmudgeon was also the only one who read the safety manual.
Every curmudgeon believes the world got worse the year he stopped enjoying it.
A cursory glance missed the clause that later cost two million.
Cursory shares a root with "course": the eye runs over the page without stopping.
The trip was curtailed by weather and one extremely persuasive harbormaster.
Rights are rarely abolished; they are curtailed, quietly, in appendices.
He was too cynical to be surprised and too curious to stop investigating.
The original Cynics were philosophers who lived in barrels; the modern kind live on committees.
